content.title: Why Priority Matters
content.description: In many real-world systems, tasks are not processed in arrival order. Instead, higher-priority tasks are executed first.

content.content: Traditional queues follow the FIFO (First In First Out) principle. However, many applications such as operating systems, job schedulers, emergency services, and graph algorithms require processing elements based on priority rather than insertion order.

content.title: Real-Life Examples
content.content: Hospital emergency rooms, CPU scheduling, flight control systems, network routing, and search engines use priority-based processing.
What is a Priority Queue?

content.definition: A data structure where each element has a priority, and elements with higher priority are processed before lower-priority elements.

content.content: Unlike a normal queue, removal is based on priority rather than insertion order.

content.title: Priority Queue Example
steps: Task B → Task A → Task C

content.title: Key Idea
content.description: Highest-priority element is always removed first.

content.content: Applications of Priority Queues

items.question: CPU Scheduling
items.answer: High-priority processes get CPU access first.

items.question: Hospital Emergency Systems
items.answer: Critical patients are treated before others.

items.question: Graph Algorithms
items.answer: Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms use Priority Queues.

content.content: What is a Heap?
A Heap is a specialized complete binary tree used to efficiently implement Priority Queues.

content.definition: A Complete Binary Tree that satisfies the Heap Property.

content.title: Important Property
content.content: Heaps are usually implemented using arrays instead of pointer-based tree structures.
Complete Binary Tree
Before understanding heaps, it is important to understand Complete Binary Trees.

content.definition: A tree where all levels are completely filled except possibly the last level, which is filled from left to right.

content.content: Types of Heaps

items.question: Max Heap
items.answer: Parent node is always greater than or equal to its children.

items.question: Min Heap
items.answer: Parent node is always smaller than or equal to its children.

content.content: Max Heap
In a Max Heap, the largest element is always stored at the root.

content.title: Observation
content.content: Root always contains the maximum value.
Min Heap
In a Min Heap, the smallest element is always stored at the root.

content.title: Observation
content.content: Root always contains the minimum value.
Array Representation of Heap
Since heaps are Complete Binary Trees, they can be efficiently stored inside arrays.
Insertion in Heap
New elements are inserted at the next available position and then moved upward to restore heap order.
Deletion from Heap
Deleting the root element requires replacing it with the last node and restoring heap order.
Heapify Operation
Heapify restores the heap property when a node violates heap ordering.
Build Heap
A heap can be constructed efficiently from an unsorted array using repeated heapify operations.
Heap Sort
Heap Sort uses a heap to repeatedly extract the largest (or smallest) element and produce a sorted sequence.

items.answer: Find largest or smallest K elements efficiently.

content.content: Complexity Summary

content.title: Interview Tip
content.content: Whenever a problem asks for Top K elements, Kth largest/smallest value, task scheduling, or dynamic maximum/minimum tracking, think about using a Heap.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: Priority Queues and Heaps are among the most frequently tested data structures in coding interviews because they provide efficient solutions for optimization and scheduling problems.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Priority Queues process elements by priority.
Max Heap stores largest element at root.
Min Heap stores smallest element at root.
Heap Sort takes O(n log n).
Top-K and scheduling problems often use Heaps.
